slides: Let's continue. First a number that leaves, and then the biggest and the smallest possible values.

slides.say: The balance works the same when a number leaves. The average of a group is fifty. One number, eighty, leaves. Now the average is forty-five. How many numbers are left?
This time eighty was in the old group, so we compare it to the old average. Eighty minus fifty is thirty. So eighty is thirty above.
The numbers that are left have an average of forty-five. Fifty minus forty-five is five. So each one is five below fifty.
The eighty was thirty above fifty. So those left must be thirty below fifty together. Each counts as five below. Thirty divided by five is six. So six numbers are left.
Let's check. Six times forty-five is two hundred seventy. Plus eighty is three hundred fifty. And seven numbers with an average of fifty also give seven times fifty, three hundred fifty.
So in the balance, we compare the number to the average of the group it is in. Joins, the new average. Leaves, the old average.
Now a different kind of question. Five positive whole numbers have an average of ten. What's the biggest possible value of one of them?
First the sum. Five numbers, average ten. Five times ten is fifty.
To make one number as big as it can be, we make the other four as small as they can be.
The smallest positive whole number is one. So the other four are one each. One plus one plus one plus one is four.
So the big one gets the rest. Fifty minus four is forty-six.
Now careful. If the question says the numbers are different, we can't use four ones. The four smallest different positive whole numbers are one, two, three and four.
One plus two plus three plus four is ten. So the big one is fifty minus ten, forty.
So watch the words positive, whole and different. Each one changes the answer.
And the opposite question. In five days, Dan made twenty-two phone calls. On one day he made more calls than on any other day. At least how many calls did he make on that day?
The average is twenty-two divided by five. That's more than four and less than five. The busiest day is at least the average, so it's at least five.
Let's try five. Then every other day had fewer calls, so at most four.
So five calls on the busiest day, and four other days with four calls each. Four times four is sixteen, plus five is twenty-one. That's less than twenty-two, so five is not enough.
Let's try six. The other four days can have four calls each. Six plus four plus four plus four plus four is twenty-two. Six is more than every other day, so the answer is six.
So for the biggest possible value, make the others as small as they can be. For the smallest possible biggest value, make the others as big as they can be.
at: value, make the others as big

Each new value is eight plus five, thirteen. All three are thirteen, so their average is thirteen.
It agrees with the last lesson. Every value grew by five, so the average grew by five.
